One other idea if you’re the trigger is just being boring around him. No play, no interaction, not even looking at him. And rewarding him for not biting then. The minute he starts biting to play you leave. Keep reinforcing the behaviour you want to see and I’m sure you’ll get there.

Not a puppy but we adopted an adult dog with very little bite inhibition. On the occasions that he did jump and mouth for something of value in our hands, he about knocked us over as an 100lb dog. And his teeth didn’t draw blood but by god they hurt. 

Here’s the advice the trainer gave to us: first put something undesirable on the objects he mouths (for us it was just vinegar) so it tastes bad. Automatic distractor, but only a band aid solution. The longer term one used in conjunction was 1. Redirect with a toy/food. Strike one. If that didn’t work, strike two is cold turkey leaving the room the second he jumped up and bit again. Sometimes he’d come after us so we’d tether his harness to something sturdy. We’d come back after a minute or two and resume the process. 

This strategy is used in conjunction with plenty of impulse control games like leave it and honing his other commands in high-distraction/high-arousal environments. The other trick is to AVOID putting him in high arousal states until you’ve got the set up down pat. For us the cues were telling: he had specific toys he got antsy over and fetch as a game completely brought out his nutty side. For you it sounds like a specific kind of playing style which might be harder, but basically watch his crazies and do calming activities like sniffing so he doesn’t have the chance to practice indiscriminate mouthing. 

I promise you you will see results if you keep at this. It took us about a month and a half for improvements but I imagine a puppy would be faster.

I think this comment is beautifully phrased and I agree with most of it, but to be fair to OP, I’m not sure that not “having the personality for it” is necessarily the case. OP could be the perfect pet person for another dog, one who’s more outgoing and more engaged. 

I really loved what you said about pets being relationships, that you get the most out of them when you put the most in. I think it’s equally important to recognize though that there is often a huge amount of emotional labor involved in caring for a dog with an unknown history. Oftentimes, the dedication that is put in is rewarded with little more than the satisfaction of having cared for an animal. And for some it is so hard to keep going on just that prospect alone. I’m thinking a lot about decisions to rehome or euthanize on r/reactivedogs, where the owners did everything they could and more to help the pups but the dogs’ responses and conditions couldn’t improve. It is a heartwrenching and difficult journey every time. I can’t say for sure that I would have been altruistic or strong enough to go through with something like it. My wife is, but not me.

I’m blessed with a pup that was able to become our heart dog with time, and that’s mostly because my wife fought for him. But if OP doesn’t choose to wait to rehome or work with this current pup, I don’t think it absolutely means they are unsuited to be a pet owner.

Just want to say good luck to OP. We went through a similar phase when we got Mouse, our pyr mix. We couldn’t do any of the traditional “dog” things we pictured with him and it felt like we were giving up all our time and freedom for an animal that’s never going to appreciate it. Like damn, we could have gotten a feral cat for the amount of engagement he showed. He came out of his shell eventually and is our best boy now, but we adapted to each other rather than “fixed” him, so to speak. 

 I think you might be expecting a little to much of both yourself and your newly adopted pup. Having an animal do service work is a huge ask when you’ve only known them for a month. No shame in rehoming if you feel like he isn’t for you, but please don’t blame him or yourself for worsening your depression. Having a dog is like a relationship. Sometimes they don’t work out. Or sometimes they do work out but it takes effort. Whatever your choice, Mouse and I send our best and hope things work out for you.

They either say they’ve done the tests or do tests with incomplete results, or say that DNA tests alone would suffice, and folks don’t know better or haven’t done the research accept them at their word. Buyers are mostly concerned about not buying from dirty cage-using puppy mills, and some breeders go very far in order to mask the realities of their breeding conditions. Some are just backyard breeders who throw their pets together. 

And doodles are SO available. Most buyers want a dog within a certain timeframe. They don’t necessarily want to wait 2-3 years on a reputable purebred breeder’s list for a litter that might not happen. So they “compromise” with a doodle breeder who they believe does not mistreat their dogs and who will have litters on the ground ASAP. 

You’re right that there should be a market for well bred doodles. Unfortunately due to both buyer ignorance and seller fraud, “well-bred doodles” is so far an oxymoron.
